title: Improving Air Quality When Moving Into a New Home
h1: How Do You Improve Air Quality When Moving Into a New Home?
description: Steps to improve indoor air quality when moving into a new home: filters, duct cleaning, ventilation, HVAC checks and what to do before the furniture arrives.
quick_answer: Start before the furniture arrives. Change the HVAC filter, have the ducts and system inspected and cleaned if needed, air out the house, and check the dryer vent, exhaust fans and smoke and carbon monoxide alarms. These steps clear out the previous owner's dust, pet dander and odors before you settle in.
body:
Why does a new-to-you home have air quality issues?

Every home carries some history. Previous owners may have had pets, smoked, done a remodel or let the filter go for a long time. Even a freshly painted house can have fumes from new paint, flooring and cabinets.

The HVAC system collects all of that. Dust, dander and odors settle in the ducts and on the coil, then get blown back out when you turn the system on. Moving itself kicks up more dust as boxes and furniture come in.

What should you do before you move in?

An empty house is the easiest time to work on the air. If you can, take care of these first:

  1. Replace the HVAC filter. Note the size and set a reminder for the next change.
  2. Have the ducts inspected. Look for heavy dust, pet hair, construction debris or rodent signs. If they're dirty, cleaning before your things arrive is much easier.
  3. Schedule an HVAC check. A technician can clean the coil and blower, check the condensate drain, look at the furnace venting and tell you how old the equipment is.
  4. Clean the dryer vent. Lint buildup is a fire hazard, and you don't know when it was last cleaned.
  5. Test smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, and replace any that are old or missing.
  6. Peek into the attic for droppings, matted insulation or disconnected ducts.

How do you deal with odors from previous owners?

Pet and smoke odors stick to surfaces, including the inside of ducts and the coil. Cleaning carpets and walls helps, but if the smell returns every time the AC runs, it's likely coming from the system.

A thorough duct cleaning, coil cleaning and a fresh filter take care of most of it. For stubborn odors, a carbon filter or an in-duct air purifier can help with what's left.

Do you need to replace the HVAC system right away?

Usually not. Unless the inspection turns up a cracked heat exchanger, a failing compressor or equipment that clearly isn't working, a cleaning and tune-up is enough to start. Ask the technician how old the system is and what condition it's in, so you can plan for a replacement in the next few years instead of being surprised by one in the middle of summer.

If the system is old and the ducts are torn or crushed, it can make sense to plan duct replacement and equipment replacement together down the road.

What about paint and new material fumes?

Fresh paint, new carpet, vinyl flooring and pressed-wood cabinets give off fumes that are strongest in the first days and weeks. Ventilation is the best tool.

  • Open windows when the weather allows. Most of the year, San Diego and Orange County weather makes that easy.
  • Run bathroom and kitchen exhaust fans.
  • Run the HVAC fan to keep air moving through the filter.
  • Skip air fresheners, which add more chemicals instead of removing them.

On wildfire smoke or heavy Santa Ana dust days, keep windows closed and rely on the filter instead.

What should you check in the first few months?

Once you've settled in, keep an eye on a few things:

  • How fast the filter gets dirty. Very fast loading can point to leaky return ducts.
  • Musty smells when the AC runs, which can mean moisture at the coil or in the ducts.
  • Humidity. Coastal homes may need help keeping it down, and inland homes can get very dry during Santa Ana winds.
  • Rooms that are much hotter or colder than others, which can mean duct leaks or crushed ducts.

Is duct cleaning worth it for a new home?

If you don't know the home's history, it's one of the best times to do it. You get a look inside the ducts and a clean start, and it's far easier before furniture and rugs are in place.

Our air duct cleaning includes an inspection first. If you'd like help with filters, purifiers or humidity, our indoor air quality team can set up the system for how you'll live in the home.
faqs: Should I clean the air ducts in a newly built home?

New construction often leaves drywall dust, sawdust and debris in the ducts, especially if the system ran during building. Ask the builder whether vents were covered during construction. If not, or if you see dust blowing from vents, an inspection and cleaning is a good idea.
How soon should I change the HVAC filter after moving in?
Right away. You don't know how long the current filter has been in. Check it again after a month, since moving stirs up dust, then follow the schedule for your filter type and household.
Is it safe to sleep in a freshly painted room?

Many people do so once the paint is dry, especially with low-VOC paint, but airing the room out for a day or two first is sensible. Keep windows open when you can and run fans. Anyone sensitive to odors, plus young children, may do better waiting a bit longer.
What should I ask the sellers about the HVAC system?

Ask how old the equipment is, when it was last serviced, when the filter was last changed, whether the ducts have ever been cleaned or replaced, and whether there have been pest, leak or mold problems. Any service records are helpful to have.
